organizations.name: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
aliases: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team (Monitoring Team)
organizations.notes: Authors the report on al-Qaeda, ISIL and associated groups. It gathers information from member states and habitually avoids accusing member states directly.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: Caliph is disputed. The General Directorate of Provinces (GDP) is roughly equivalent to al-Qaeda's general manager. Five key regional offices: Al-Karrar, Al-Furqan, Al-Siddiq, and the Syria and Iraq provinces.

organizations.name: Al-Karrar office
organizations.notes: ISIS regional office coordinating recruiting, fundraising and funneling of money and war material to Africa, Afghanistan, Yemen and Turkey. Headed by Mumin and reportedly ISIS's most important financial stream.

organizations.name: ISIS-Somalia
organizations.notes: Growing in numbers, with 300-500 fighters recruited from Yemen and East/North Africa. It pushed al-Shabaab out of part of the Al Miskaad mountains in Puntland.

organizations.name: ISIS-Yemen
organizations.notes: Weak; linked to ISIS-Somalia via a smuggling network

organizations.name: al-Shabaab
organizations.notes: Called the 'Taliban of Africa'. It funds other al-Qaeda branches and remits money to al-Qaeda leadership. It is reportedly seeking 3D-printed weapons and weaponized drones.

organizations.name: Jaysh Ayman
organizations.notes: Armed wing operating in Kenya and southern Somalia

organizations.name: Amniyat
organizations.notes: al-Shabaab's intelligence/security wing

organizations.name: AQAP
organizations.notes: In a truce or deconfliction period with the Houthis. Possible internal divisions after the deaths of Batarfi and Saif al-Adel's son.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Leader Saif al-Adel is reportedly in Iran. It sent a Somali-linked operative to Iraq to set up cells.

organizations.name: JNIM
organizations.notes: Controls about 40% of Burkina Faso (Nov 2023 estimate). It has non-aggression pacts with some Tuareg factions, a fragile truce with ISGS, and is expanding south into Benin and Togo.

organizations.name: Islamic State Sahel Province
aliases: Islamic State in the Greater Sahara
organizations.notes: Strong in Menaka, Gao, Tillaberi and eastern Burkina Faso. It is linking up with the Lake Chad theatre.

organizations.name: Al-Furqan office
organizations.notes: Now covers West Africa, the Sahel and North Africa, having absorbed the former office responsible for Egypt and Sudan and, earlier, Libya's Al-Anfal office.

organizations.name: Al-Siddiq office
organizations.notes: ISIS regional office for Afghanistan; the report mainly discusses ISKP

organizations.name: ISKP
organizations.notes: Seen as the leading immediate terror threat in non-conflict zones. It uses Tajik, Uzbek and other Central Asian diasporas and has a Turkey connection (Crocus City attackers, Moscow, March 2024).

organizations.name: ISIS Central Africa Province
organizations.notes: Resilient despite Operation Shujaa. It recruits from Sudan, Tanzania and Somalia.

organizations.name: ISIS Mozambique
organizations.notes: 250-350 fighters; shifting to Dawa and civilian outreach

organizations.name: Operation Shujaa
organizations.notes: Joint DRC-Uganda operation across three agreed sectors

organizations.name: Hayat Tahrir al-Sham
organizations.notes: Led by al-Jolani. Broke from al-Qaeda but still provides logistical support to Hurras al-Din.

organizations.name: Hurras al-Din
organizations.notes: al-Qaeda's branch in Syria

organizations.name: Tuareg rebels
organizations.notes: Started the recent attack that killed about 50 Wagner mercenaries; JNIM joined

organizations.name: Wagner Group
organizations.notes: About 50 Wagner mercenaries killed in northern Mali a few days before the episode

organizations.name: US Treasury
organizations.notes: In 2022 designated a smuggling network between northern Somalia and Yemen serving al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia

organizations.name: Houthis
organizations.notes: US reports al-Shabaab is seeking sophisticated weapons from them

organizations.name: Iran
organizations.notes: Hosts Saif al-Adel and al-Qaeda leaders; the report does not say so explicitly

organizations.name: Turkey
organizations.notes: Turkey is a hub for ISIS finance and facilitation. It claimed about a year ago to have captured the ISIS leader, which appeared untrue.

organizations.name: Hezbollah
organizations.notes: Mentioned as active in Syria alongside Iran.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Described, along with al-Qaeda, as playing footsies with Pakistan and Iran, which can push fervent jihadists to IS.

organizations.name: Shia militias (Iraq/Syria)
organizations.notes: Their attacks on US bases likely reduced counterterrorism operations.

organizations.name: General Directorate of Provinces
organizations.notes: IS body that links regional offices and provinces.

organizations.name: Darod clan
organizations.notes: Somali clan family of Abdul Qadir Mumin; claims Qurayshi descent (hosts call this myth).

key_claims: The hosts doubt that Abdul Qadir Mumin is the ISIS caliph, but he is at least head of the Al-Karrar office and likely of the General Directorate of Provinces.
ISIS-Somalia and the Al-Karrar office are growing and are now a central financial stream for ISIS globally, using the Somali diaspora and hawala networks.
ISIS-Somalia has pushed al-Shabaab out of part of the Al Miskaad mountains, and al-Shabaab may see this as an existential threat.
JNIM controls about 40% of Burkina Faso and is expanding into Benin and Togo, aided by coups, Wagner and weak local governance.
The Al-Furqan office now oversees West Africa, the Sahel and North Africa and is linking with ISGS via northwestern Nigeria and Niger.
ISKP is the leading terror threat in non-conflict zones, using Central Asian diasporas and routes through Turkey.
The report avoids saying explicitly that Saif al-Adel is in Iran and understates Turkey's role.
Al-Qaeda is trying to build cells in Iraq and HTS still supports Hurras al-Din.
Saif al-Adel is in Iran as a guest of the Iranian government, yet the UN report never says so explicitly.
The report says al-Qaeda sent a man named 'Somali' to Iraq to set up cells, which shows al-Qaeda sees opportunity there.
HTS broke from al-Qaeda but still provides logistical support to al-Qaeda's Syrian branch Hurras al-Din.
The deaths of AQAP leader Khalid Batarfi and Saif al-Adel's son raise suspicions of internal disputes, and some member states think AQAP is divided.
Edmund Fitton-Brown speculates that Saif al-Adel's son pushed AQAP into a truce with the Houthis, which may have angered jihadis in Yemen and could help IS recruit.
Al-Qaeda's alliances of convenience, such as hosting by Iran and Taliban dealings with Pakistan and Iran, can push fervent jihadists toward the Islamic State.
The Islamic State is devolving control to regional offices and provinces, so it is becoming a more integrated but globally dispersed organization like al-Qaeda.
ISKP could mount a major attack in Western Europe in 2024, while al-Qaeda plays a longer game, including the 'Afghanization' of Somalia and the Sahel.
